title: Rafts and log floats

names.gloss: to float, as a log on the water

identification.basis: Roth's 1910 transport bulletin records the log raft of the Tully to Mulgrave scrub people, the V-raft of the Wellesley Islands, the log float of the Mitchell River mouth and the pandanus-log swimming of the Keppels, with figures and photographs; no Kuku Yalanji raft is recorded, and the dictionary has only the words for log, float and swim.

summary: A raft is what a river in flood gets when there is no [canoe](entry:canoes): 'these log-rafts are used rather in times of flood than at others, and are generally discarded after use' [ref:roth1910]. The dictionary has the parts, **[walmba](word:walmba)** 'log' and **[walngkal](word:walngkal)** 'to float, as a log on the water', and **[mariji-y](word:mariji-y)** 'to swim across or through water', but no word for the raft itself, and Roth records none on Kuku Yalanji country: the log raft he drew was the *warra-jan* of the lower Tully, 'met with among the scrub-blacks from the Tully to the Russell and Mulgrave Rivers' [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1910]. Four or five light logs, cut off blunt, tied afloat with lawyer cane at the two ends only, a scrap of teatree bark and sand at one end to carry a fire, and a pole to steer and punt with: that is the whole craft, and his figure of the lashing is on this page [ref:roth1910]. Far down the Mitchell, 'at the mouth of the Mitchell River', the crossing tool was a single log of some very light tree, five or six feet long, straddled 'somewhat in the position of a child riding a hobby-horse', one hand to balance and one free for the spears [ref:roth1910].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[walmba](word:walmba)** 'log'; on the Endeavour River Roth recorded the same word for a log laid across a creek as a bridge [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1910]. **[walngkal](word:walngkal)** 'to hang; to float, as a log on the water'; **[mariji-y](word:mariji-y)** 'to swim; to swim across or through water'; **[kalka](word:kalka)** 'fishing spear, also generic term for spear', the thing kept dry on the float [ref:hershberger1982]. The Tully (Mallanpara) raft was *warra-jan*, of the timbers *ponol* and *pedu* (*Grewia pleiostigma*) [ref:roth1910]. No Kuku Yalanji word for a raft is on record.

sections.heading: The rafts Roth recorded
sections.body:
**The log raft of the scrub country.** 'Log-rafts are met with among the scrub-blacks from the Tully to the Russell and Mulgrave Rivers, the coastal ones employing bark-canoes. On the Lower Tully, amongst the Mallanpara Tribe, the raft or *warra-jan* is manufactured of two kinds of timber, the *ponol* and the *pedu* (*Grewia pleiostigma*). Four, sometimes five logs of one or other material, are cut off blunt at each end, no attempt being made at pointing them so as to better resist the friction of the water, and tied, while afloat, with a length of lawyer-cane at the two ends only. The tying consists of two parts; first round the outside logs, and fixing the cane at any spot suitable; and secondly, fixing together the upper and under portions of the cane itself, as well as the intermediate logs, by what may be called a frapping turn. This is effected with another cane ... which after being tightened up at the first interspace, has its extremities brought over through the next interval, tightening up again, and passing through the last intervening space, where it is finally fixed' (his fig. 2, on this page). 'These log-rafts are used rather in times of flood than at others, and are generally discarded after use. Sometimes there are a few small pieces of timber placed crosswise at one extremity, and on them a piece of tea-tree bark, sand, etc., may be laid; a fire can thus be kept burning. So far as the shape of the raft is concerned, sometimes the outer, sometimes the inner logs project; there is certainly no attempt at uniformity or any approach to making a bow or stern. No blade or paddle is used for its propulsion, only a pole which can both steer and punt it. It can be worked by one or two occupants; in the latter case with a pole on either side' [ref:roth1910].

**The log float of the Mitchell.** 'At the mouth of the Mitchell River, and some of the rivers to the south of it, as well as, I am told, on a few of the creeks to the northward, the cut trunk of some very light tree (? White Mangrove) is utilised as a float. Such a log is cut to about between five and six feet long, and when in the water can easily support the native who stretches himself upon it straddle-leg, with the thicker butt-end in front, somewhat in the position of a child riding a hobby-horse, and so paddles himself along; being able to keep his balance with the one hand, he can thus have the other free to carry his spears, etc. To see these logs for the first time, lying as they were here and there on the sides of the river-banks, and to suggest the purpose for which they were intended, would certainly have constituted a puzzle' [ref:roth1910]. The mouth of the Mitchell is Kokoberra and Yir Yoront country, a long way downstream of Karma Waters, on the same river [ref:roth1910].

**The V-raft of the Wellesley Islands.** 'It is V-shaped, composed of numerous light saplings ("White Mangrove") with butts all at one end, the larger logs underneath and at the sides, all tied together fore and aft, a cross-tie connecting the two loops to prevent them from slipping; over the wider portion of the raft is placed a bundle of dried grass, upon which the traveller squats and paddles himself along' (his Plate II, on this page) [ref:roth1910].

**The swimming log of the Keppels.** Keppel Islanders crossed six miles of sea in a chain behind 'a pandanus log, up to as much as thirteen or fourteen feet in length, according to the number in the party': the leader guided its end with one hand and swam with the other, 'the man behind, resting his right hand on number one's loins propels himself with his left; number three holds onto number two with his left, and swims with his right, and so on'; when the leader tired another took his place, 'and if all require a few minutes' rest, they have the float to hold on to' [ref:roth1910].

sections.heading: Raft, float, canoe, trough
sections.body:
- **A log raft** carries two people and a fire across a flood and is left on the far bank [ref:roth1910].
- **A log float** carries one swimmer and his spears [ref:roth1910].
- **A [bark trough](entry:bark-troughs)** or wooden vessel pushed ahead of a swimmer carries the gear: impedimenta went 'in a bark or dug-out wooden vessel propelled in front of them' [ref:roth1910].
- **A [canoe](entry:canoes)** is a made thing kept for years; a raft is a flood's thing [ref:roth1910].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **Cut light logs lying on the river bank**, 'here and there', were Roth's puzzle at the Mitchell mouth: floats waiting [ref:roth1910].
- **A raft on the far bank** after a flood, its cane lashings cut or rotting [ref:roth1910].
- **A pandanus log** on a beach with the bark worn smooth [ref:roth1910].
- **Floating things that are usable**, *yanday*, washed up after the wet: raft timber [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Timber
sections.body: Light wood that floats high: the Tully rafts were *Grewia* and *ponol*, the Mitchell floats and the Wellesley rafts 'White Mangrove', the Keppel logs pandanus [ref:roth1910]. The dictionary's *yanday*, 'things that float up on the beach such as timber, usable things only', is the flood's own supply [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: The raft and the flood
sections.body: The raft belongs to the wet, when the rivers run bank to bank and the fords are gone; see [seasons](entry:seasons). It is the flood answer to the problem the [canoe](entry:canoes) page sets out: 'a river in flood is met by diving across close to the bottom, where the natives say the current is never so strong', or by a log, or by a raft, or by waiting [ref:roth1910]. The [crocodiles](entry:freshwater-crocodile) move with the flood too, and the tidal rivers have the [other one](entry:saltwater-crocodile), which is why a crossing on a log was a thing done with care and company [ref:roth1910].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Flood time: the raft is 'used rather in times of flood than at others' [ref:roth1910]. The rest of the year the river is forded: 'as a matter of choice, the native will rather wade across a stream than go to the exertion of swimming it' [ref:roth1910]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- Crossing a flooded river with a fire and two people [ref:roth1910].
- Swimming a river with spears kept dry, on a log float [ref:roth1910].
- Carrying gear across a stream in a bark or wooden vessel pushed ahead [ref:roth1910].
- Crossing to islands, on the Wellesleys and the Keppels [ref:roth1910].

sections.heading: Making a log raft and a log float
sections.body:
**The log raft** (Tully method) [ref:roth1910]:

1. **Cut four or five logs** of a light timber, the same length, blunt at both ends; no pointing [ref:roth1910].
2. **Float them** side by side in the shallows; the raft is tied afloat, not on the bank [ref:roth1910].
3. **First lashing**, at each end: a length of lawyer cane round the two outside logs, over the top and under the bottom, fixed where convenient [ref:roth1910].
4. **Second lashing**, the frapping turn: with another cane, pass between the first and second logs, pulling the upper and lower runs of the first cane together and tightening; bring the ends over through the next gap and tighten again; through the last gap and fix. Each log is now gripped between the two runs of cane (Roth's fig. 2) [ref:roth1910].
5. **Fire**: lay a few sticks across one end, teatree bark on them, sand on the bark, and the fire on the sand [ref:roth1910].
6. **Pole it**: no paddle; one person with a pole, or two with a pole each side, steering and punting [ref:roth1910].
7. **Leave it** on the far bank; it was made for this flood [ref:roth1910].

**The log float** (Mitchell mouth) [ref:roth1910]: cut a trunk of a very light tree five or six feet long; in the water, lie along it straddle-legged with the thick butt in front; balance with one hand and paddle with it; carry the spears in the other.

**The swimming chain** (Keppels) [ref:roth1910]: a long light log; the leader guides the thin end with one hand and swims with the other; each swimmer behind holds the one in front with one hand and swims with the other; change leaders when tired; rest on the log.

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- A flood is not the time to learn; a raft was the last resort of people who could all swim, and 'a river in flood is met by diving across close to the bottom' only by those who knew it [ref:roth1910].
- Crocodiles: 'the Princess Charlotte Bay Natives never consider it safe to swim even silently on the surface of these waters, however clear they may be, when crocodiles are about' [ref:roth1910]. See [crocodiles](entry:crocodiles).
- Lashings tied afloat with green cane loosen as the cane dries; retie before a second crossing [ref:roth1910].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: A four-log raft tied afloat is an afternoon's work and a way to learn the lashing, in the dry, on a quiet pool [ref:roth1910]. No Kuku Yalanji raft or float is on record; if the Western Yalanji had one, or a word for it, the contribution box below is for that [ref:hershberger1982].

locations.summary: **No raft or log float is recorded for the Hann River country.** The nearest written records of crossing water are Roth's from the lower Normanby, downstream at Princess Charlotte Bay, where crocodile rivers were crossed by diving [ref:roth1910]. The Hann is a spring-fed river that has not stopped flowing since its gauge opened in 1968: a flood river in the wet, a low clear run between deep holes in the late dry [ref:bom-105001b] [ref:wetlandinfo-normanby].

sections.heading: When the Hann has to be crossed
sections.body:
**Wet, December to March.** 'During the peak of the wet season (December to March), heavy rains cause the rivers to flood' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. At the Sandy Creek gauge the Hann runs highest in February and March, a mean of about 20–22 m³/s; the biggest daily mean on record was about 430 m³/s, on 12 February 1974 [ref:bom-105001b]. Rinyirru's roads close in the wet, 'usually December to May' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-2013].

**Dry.** By September to November the river is down to about 0.3–0.4 m³/s [ref:bom-105001b]. It is then a low, clear run between deep holes, fed by springs, never dry sand [ref:wetlandinfo-normanby].

sections.heading: How people crossed water here
sections.body:
**Lower Normanby (Princess Charlotte Bay), Roth, about 1900.** Where 'a known crocodile-infested river has to be crossed, and there is no canoe, the black manages it by diving', close to the bottom, stirring up the mud if a crocodile comes. Lily-seed divers had a friend watching from the bank [ref:roth1910]. Roth adds, without naming a district, that 'a river in flood is met by diving across close to the bottom, where the natives say the current is never so strong' [ref:roth1910].

**Kuku Thaypan.** Elder Dr George Musgrave told of the messmate, *Ku Aldkalemba*: you take its bark 'only get certain time after wet' to make a humpy, and 'you can make canoe out of him'; it also made a dish, *Karoll* [ref:standley2019]. See [canoes](entry:canoes). No Kuku Thaypan raft is described.

sections.heading: Safety here
sections.body: Both crocodiles live in this river system; treat every deep hole on the Hann as saltwater crocodile water. See [crocodiles](entry:crocodiles) for the Hann River in full.

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The upper Hann is the Possum People's country [ref:fca-possum]; the middle and lower Hann are in the Thaypan native title determination of November 2023, held by the Awu-Laya Indigenous Corporation [ref:fca-thaypan]. Ask them before using their timber or their river.

locations.summary: The Mitchell at [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) still floods every wet and still has light timber on its banks after every flood [ref:roth1910] [ref:kw-camping]. Flood time here is December to April [ref:bom-palmerville].

sections.heading: Timber here
sections.body: At [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) the [pandanus](entry:pandanus) of the river banks and the dead light timber of the flood line are the candidates, with [lawyer cane](entry:lawyer-cane) or any strong vine for the lashing [ref:roth1910].

sections.heading: Safety here
sections.body:
- On the freshwater Mitchell, the deep pools at dusk are the freshwater crocodile's [ref:kw-about].
- The station's advice on the river in the wet is the same as Roth's: wait [ref:kw-camping].

locations.summary: On the Bloomfield the camps moved to the ridges in the wet; the [seasons](entry:seasons) page says why [ref:anderson1996]. The records from this coast are of troughs pushed ahead of a swimmer, and of the timber-getters' rafts.

sections.heading: How people crossed water here
sections.body:
On the Bloomfield the bigger [bark troughs](entry:bark-troughs) were 'used for carrying infants and other impedimenta across creeks, by being pushed along in front of the swimmer' [ref:roth1904].

When the timber-getters came, the red cedar logs of the Daintree went down to the coast on lashed rafts: a timber raft was the European version, for moving timber downriver [ref:wiki-daintree].
